client: Hey Luna, I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately. The pressure to excel in my graduate program is intense, and I'm also trying to keep up with my part-time job at the coffee shop. I don't know how much longer I can keep this up, and I'm starting to doubt if therapy can really help with all this.
therapist: Hi there, it sounds like you're under a lot of pressure and feeling overwhelmed. It’s completely understandable to doubt your ability to keep up with everything, and it’s okay to feel this way. Can you tell me more about what specific thoughts or feelings come up when you think about your workload and responsibilities?

client: When I think about everything I have to do, I feel this knot in my stomach and a constant sense of dread. I worry that I’m not good enough and that I’m going to fail. It’s hard to see a way out, and I keep thinking that no matter what I do, it won’t be enough.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a heavy emotional burden, and the sense of dread and worry are really weighing on you. Those feelings of not being good enough and fearing failure can be incredibly tough to manage. What are some of the thoughts that come up most frequently when you feel this way, and how do they affect your day-to-day?

client: I often think, "I can’t do this" or "I’m going to mess up." These thoughts make it hard to focus on my work, and I find myself procrastinating because I’m so anxious. It’s a vicious cycle, and I feel like I’m just spinning my wheels.
therapist: It’s really tough when those negative thoughts keep coming up and make it hard to focus. The anxiety and sense of being stuck can be overwhelming. Can you think of any small steps or strategies that might help break this cycle, even if just a little bit? For example, is there a specific task you could start with that feels more manageable?

client: I appreciate the suggestion, but it’s hard to see anything as manageable right now. Everything feels like a mountain to climb. I guess I could try to break down my tasks into smaller steps, but I worry that I’ll just get overwhelmed again and not make any progress.
therapist: I can really understand how overwhelming everything feels right now, like every task is a huge mountain to climb. Breaking things down into smaller steps is a good strategy, even if it doesn’t feel like it will make a big difference at first. What do you think might help you stay motivated or feel a sense of progress, even with these smaller steps? Maybe there’s a way to reward yourself or acknowledge the small victories?

client: I like the idea of rewarding myself for small victories, but it’s hard to feel motivated when I’m so anxious. Maybe I could try something simple, like taking a short walk or treating myself to a favorite snack after completing a small task. I just hope it’s enough to keep me going and not feel so overwhelmed.
therapist: It’s great that you’re considering ways to reward yourself for those small victories. Taking a short walk or enjoying a favorite snack can definitely help create a sense of accomplishment and motivation. It’s okay if it feels like a small step; every bit of progress counts. How do you think you can remind yourself to take these breaks and rewards, especially when you’re feeling anxious and overwhelmed?

client: I think setting reminders on my phone might help. That way, I won’t forget to take those breaks and reward myself. But I’m still a bit skeptical because when I’m really anxious, I tend to ignore those reminders and push through, thinking it will help me get more done.
therapist: Setting reminders on your phone is a practical step, and it’s great that you’re thinking about ways to support yourself. It’s understandable to feel skeptical, especially when anxiety makes it hard to follow through. Sometimes, acknowledging that it’s okay to take breaks—even when you’re anxious—can help. What do you think might make it easier to follow through with those reminders, even when you’re feeling really anxious?

client: I think it might help if I can remind myself that taking breaks isn’t a sign of weakness, but a way to recharge and be more productive. It’s hard to internalize that, though, especially when the anxiety is so strong. Maybe if I write down some positive affirmations or reasons why breaks are important, it could help me stick to the reminders.
therapist: That’s a really insightful approach. Recognizing that breaks are a way to recharge and not a sign of weakness is a powerful shift in mindset. Writing down positive affirmations or reasons why breaks are important can definitely help reinforce this idea. How do you think you can make these affirmations a regular part of your routine, so they become more automatic and easier to remember when you’re feeling anxious?

client: I think I could start by placing the affirmations somewhere I’ll see them often, like on my desk or on my phone’s lock screen. That way, I’ll be reminded of them throughout the day. But I’m still a bit worried that in moments of high anxiety, I might dismiss them as just words and not really believe them.
therapist: Placing the affirmations where you’ll see them often is a great idea. It can help reinforce those positive messages and make them more impactful over time. It’s totally normal to have moments where you feel like dismissing them, especially when anxiety is high. What do you think might help you connect with those affirmations more deeply, even in those tough moments? Maybe there’s a specific affirmation that resonates with you more than others?

client: I think an affirmation that resonates with me is "I am capable of handling this." It’s something I know is true, but it’s hard to believe it when I’m in the thick of anxiety. Maybe if I repeat it to myself a few times every day, it might start to feel more real. But it’s still a struggle to trust that it will make a difference.
therapist: It’s really powerful that you’ve identified an affirmation that resonates with you: "I am capable of handling this." Even if it feels hard to believe in the moment, repeating it can help reinforce that belief over time. It’s completely normal to struggle with trust and belief, especially when anxiety is high. How do you think you can make this affirmation a part of your daily routine, so it becomes a more automatic thought? Maybe there’s a specific time of day or activity where it feels more natural to repeat it?

client: I think I could repeat the affirmation in the morning when I’m getting ready for the day, and maybe again during a short break in the middle of my work. It feels a bit forced right now, but I’m willing to try. I just hope it doesn’t feel like another thing on my to-do list that adds to my stress.
therapist: It’s great that you’re willing to try incorporating the affirmation into your routine, even if it feels a bit forced at first. Starting your day with it and taking a moment during a break can be really helpful. It’s important to approach it without adding more stress, so try to see it as a gentle reminder to yourself, rather than another task. How do you think you can make this practice feel more natural and less like another to-do item? Maybe there’s a way to integrate it into a relaxing part of your routine, like while you’re having a cup of coffee or during a short walk?
